newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish police to close borders against biker gangs.
newsitem.headline: Danish police to close borders against biker gangs.

text.p: Danish police will toughen border controls in an effort to stop warring motorcycle gangs drawing reinforcments from abroad, senior officers said on Monday.

Danish and Nordic police stepped up efforts to quell violence last week after an anti-tank missile blasted a Hell's Angels clubhouse in central Copenhagen, killing two people and shocking the normally peaceful country.

It was the bloodiest single incident so far in a vicious turf war that has killed five people this year and wounded many others, in gun, bomb, grenade and rocket attacks in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden.

A memorandum to regional police chiefs from national commissioner Ivar Boye reminds them Denmark's Aliens Act can be used against allies of the Hells Angels and Bandidos gangs, both offshoots of U.S. groups with a wide European network.
"It's possible to stop people entering this country if there are security reasons, that's the law. What we have done is to tell the police districts," one officer told Reuters.
He said police must give reasons in each case for refusing entry but membership of one of the feuding groups would suffice.
Another officer said he expected the act, used to bar rowdy English football fans, to be widely applied at the land border with Germany and ferry crossings from Norway and Sweden.
Magistrates on Friday remanded until October 29 a member of a Bandidos-affiliated gang arrested during a police hunt for three men wanted for the Copenhagen rocket attack.

Investigators said they had no evidence so far directly linking the suspect with the blast in the capital but they were charging him with possession of a stolen Danish army bazooka found in the garage of a house where he had been living.
Court officials said that he denied the firearms charge and said that he did not know how the bazooka got into his garage.

Police throughout the region fear that the bikers' code of honour and rough justice will keep tit-for-tat attacks going and that a flow of combattants from neighbouring countries could escalate the conflict still further.

Tabloid newspapers at the weekend cited Hell's Angels as pledging to kill 12 Bandidos in revenge for the two victims of the October 6 clubhouse attack, itself a likely reprisal for the killing of three Bandidos over the preceeding few months.

While each gang has no more than 100 fully-fledged members in Denmark they form -- with the Outlaws and the Pagans -- the "Big Four" U.S.-based bike gangs, each able to call on a tightly-knit brotherhood of thousands of members worldwide.
Hell's Angels, the oldest and biggest of the gangs, was formed in California by restless war veterans in 1948. The Bandidos were born in Texas in 1966.
Nordic authorities are keeping a watchful eye on the Chicago-based Outlaws who have opened a branch in the Norwegian capital of Oslo.
Since the Outlaws killed three Hell's Angels in Florida in 1974 the two gangs have waged an unflagging vendetta.

The Outlaws declared themselves "proud brothers" of the Bandidos after the latter clashed with Hell's Angels' allies the Commancheros in Australia in 1984 in a pitched battle that killed seven people and injured 21.

"It's a major undertaking at the moment, with just the two sides. What we dread is a third group coming on the scene, altering the balance and presumably forcing the Hell's Angels to commit more resources to the fight," a police officer said.
